pos: n. pl. (the French Reformed Protestants of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, who endured the Wars of Religion, the Massacre of St Bartholomew, and the revocation of the Edict of Nantes)
etymology: French Huguenot, of disputed origin; often derived from Swiss German Eidgenossen, confederates, through Genevan political use. First used as a term of abuse.
biblical_def: The Huguenots were the Reformed churches of France, organised on Calvin's pattern, confessing the Gallican Confession adopted at their first national synod in Paris in 1559. At their height they were perhaps a tenth of the nation, strong among the nobility and the skilled trades, and they worshipped at the risk of their lives. They sang the metrical psalms of Marot and Beza in the streets and on the scaffold. For forty years France was torn by wars in which they fought for the right to exist; in 1572 thousands were murdered on St Bartholomew's Day; in 1598 the Edict of Nantes gave them a limited toleration; in 1685 Louis XIV revoked it. Soldiers were quartered in their homes to force conversions, pastors were banished, and some two hundred thousand fled to the Netherlands, England, Prussia, the American colonies and the Cape. They lived the word of Hebrews: “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance” (Heb 10:34). Christ had given them leave: “when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23). In France the churches of the desert met secretly in fields and caves for a century, as those “Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Huguenot as a name formerly given to the Protestants of France.
webster_full: HUGUENOT, n. A name formerly given to the Protestants of France.
HUGUENOTISM, n. The religion of the Huguenots in France.
scriptures: For ye had compassion of me in my bonds, and took joyfully the spoiling of your goods, knowing in yourselves that ye have in heaven a better and an enduring substance.
But when they persecute you in this city, flee ye into another: for verily I say unto you, Ye shall not have gone over the cities of Israel, till the Son of man be come.
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you:
corruption_summary: The Huguenots are remembered chiefly as refugees who enriched their host nations with crafts and capital; their churches remembered themselves as confessors who would not go to mass.
corruption_paragraphs: Popular history tells the Huguenot story as one of skilled immigrants — silk weavers in Spitalfields, wine-makers at the Cape, merchants in New York — and as an early chapter in the history of toleration. Both are true and both miss the centre. They left everything because they would not attend the mass or have their children baptized by priests, and they counted the loss of goods, homeland and sometimes life as nothing beside fidelity to the Reformed worship of God.

The recovery is to see them as their own psalms and sermons show them: a confessing church under the cross, worshipping by the regulative principle in fields and caves, singing the Psalms, and teaching their children the catechism in secret. Prosperity in exile was a mercy; faithfulness at home was the point.
roots_summary: Greek harpage (G724), spoiling, plunder; pheugo (G5343), to flee; planao (G4105), to wander.
usage: “took joyfully the spoiling of your goods” (Heb 10:34) — the dragonnades of 1685.
“flee ye into another” (Mat 10:23) — the refuge in the Netherlands, England and America.
“Of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb 11:38) — the church of the desert.

pos: n. (the slaughter of French Protestants that began in Paris on 24 August 1572, St Bartholomew's Day, and spread to the provinces, killing many thousands)
etymology: Named for the feast of the apostle Bartholomew on 24 August. The killing in Paris followed the wedding of the Protestant Henry of Navarre to the king's sister.
biblical_def: The St Bartholomew's Day Massacre began in the early hours of 24 August 1572. The leaders of the Huguenots had come to Paris for the marriage of Henry of Navarre to Marguerite of Valois, a wedding meant to seal peace. Two days earlier an attempt had been made on the life of Admiral Gaspard de Coligny. The royal council, Catherine de' Medici foremost, resolved to strike first. Coligny was murdered in his lodging and thrown from the window, and the city militia and mobs then hunted Protestants through the streets for days; the killing spread to Lyons, Orléans, Rouen, Toulouse and other cities through the autumn. Estimates range from several thousand to tens of thousands of dead. At Rome Pope Gregory XIII had a Te Deum sung in thanksgiving and a medal struck. Christ had foretold it: “the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2). The psalmist's lament fits the Seine: “Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them” (Psa 79:3). The souls under the altar, “slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9), were told to rest “yet for a little season” (Rev 6:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines massacre as the murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty; the indiscriminate killing of human beings without authority or necessity.
webster_full: MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers of human beings, with circumstances of cruelty; the indiscriminate killing of human beings, without authority or necessity, and without forms civil or military.
2. Murder.
scriptures: Joh 16:2
They shall put you out of the synagogues: yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service.
Psa 79:3
Their blood have they shed like water round about Jerusalem; and there was none to bury them.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Rev 6:11

And white robes were given unto every one of them; and it was said unto them, that they should rest yet for a little season, until their fellowservants also and their brethren, that should be killed as they were, should be fulfilled.
corruption_summary: The massacre is now often told as a story of court politics and religious violence on both sides; the record shows a planned killing of Protestants celebrated by the pope with a medal.
corruption_paragraphs: Recent historiography rightly attends to the faction-fighting of the French court and to the violence committed by Protestants elsewhere in the Wars of Religion. But the even-handed frame can obscure what happened in August 1572: a government and a populace murdered thousands of their neighbours because they were Reformed, and the head of the Roman church gave thanks for it publicly. Rome's medal, inscribed with the slaughter of the Huguenots, still exists.

The recovery is to remember the martyrs honestly, neither inventing atrocities nor softening real ones, and to hear in the Lord's own words why the church must expect such things: men will kill the saints thinking they serve God. The souls under the altar are not forgotten, and the Judge has not forgotten them.
roots_summary: Greek latreia (G2999), service, religious worship; Hebrew shaphak (H8210), to pour out, shed; Greek sphazo (G4969), to slay.
roots_lines: Hebrew shaphak (H8210) — to pour out, shed (blood); Psalm 79:3.
usage: “whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service” (Joh 16:2) — Paris, August 1572.
“there was none to bury them” (Psa 79:3) — the bodies in the Seine.
“slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9) — the Huguenot dead.

pos: n. (the decree of Henry IV of France in April 1598 granting the Huguenots limited freedom of worship and civil rights; revoked by Louis XIV in 1685)
etymology: Latin edictum, a proclamation; Nantes, the city in Brittany where it was signed.
biblical_def: The Edict of Nantes ended the French Wars of Religion. Henry of Navarre, once the Huguenots' leader, had become king and in 1593 conformed to Rome to secure his throne — Paris, it was said, was well worth a mass. Five years later he granted his former brethren freedom of conscience everywhere, public worship in specified places, access to offices and universities, and a number of fortified towns as security. It was the first durable settlement in Europe that allowed two confessions in one kingdom. The Huguenots used the peace well, building academies, training pastors and producing great theologians. But the edict rested on the will of a king, and kings change: “Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psa 146:3). Louis XIV revoked it in 1685 with the Edict of Fontainebleau, after years of dragoon persecution. Christians are to pray “For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty” (1Ti 2:2), knowing that “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Pro 21:1). Henry's own bargain stands under Christ's question: “what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mat 16:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines edict as that which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince to his subjects, as a rule or law requiring obedience; a proclamation of command or prohibition.
webster_full: EDICT, n. That which is uttered or proclaimed by authority as a rule of action; an order issued by a prince to his subjects, as a rule or law requiring obedience; a proclamation of command or prohibition.
2. A decree; a law.
scriptures: For kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty.
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?
corruption_summary: The Edict of Nantes is celebrated as a milestone of toleration; it was a truce granted by a king who had bought his crown with his conscience, and it lasted only as long as the crown chose.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern accounts present the edict as an early step on the road to religious liberty, and in its effect it was. But it was not grounded in a principle of liberty of conscience; it was a political settlement, a privilege conceded to a strong minority, revocable at the sovereign's pleasure. When the Huguenots were weaker and the king stronger, the privilege was withdrawn and the persecution resumed with a thoroughness the wars had not achieved.

The recovery is twofold. Christians should be grateful for every peace a ruler grants and pray for it; and they should not mistake a ruler's favour for a foundation. Liberty of conscience rests on God's lordship over the conscience, as the 1689 Confession confesses, not on an edict. And no peace is worth what Henry paid for his.
roots_summary: Greek eremos (G2263), quiet, tranquil; Hebrew batach (H982), to trust; Greek zemioo (G2210), to lose, suffer loss.
roots_lines: Greek eremos (G2263) — quiet, tranquil; 1 Timothy 2:2, the only use.
Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, be confident; Psalm 146:3.
Greek zemioo (G2210) — to suffer loss, forfeit; Matthew 16:26.
usage: “that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life” (1Ti 2:2) — the mercy of 1598.
“Put not your trust in princes” (Psa 146:3) — the lesson of 1685.
“what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world” (Mat 16:26) — Henry's mass.

pos: n. (Clément Marot, c. 1496–1544, French court poet whose metrical versions of the Psalms became the core of the Genevan Psalter)
etymology: French surname. His psalms were completed after his death by Theodore Beza; the tunes were set chiefly by Louis Bourgeois.
biblical_def: Clément Marot was valet and poet at the court of Francis I, a graceful writer of light verse who came under suspicion for evangelical sympathies and was more than once imprisoned or exiled. In the 1530s he began to render the Psalms into French verse, and they became so popular that courtiers sang them to fashionable tunes. Calvin, who wanted the congregation of Geneva to sing the Psalms in the common tongue, took up thirteen of them for his first psalter at Strasbourg in 1539. Marot came to Geneva in 1542 and finished more, so that some fifty of the hundred and fifty are his; Beza translated the rest, and the complete Genevan Psalter appeared in 1562. It put into the mouths of the French Reformed churches the apostle's command, “Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (Jas 5:13), and the psalmist's, “make a joyful noise unto him with psalms” (Psa 95:2), “sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7). Huguenot martyrs sang Marot's psalms at the stake. Marot himself, restless and unable to bear Geneva's discipline, left for Italy and died at Turin in 1544.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines psalm as a sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
webster_full: PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a song composed on a divine subject and in praise of God.
2. Appropriately, the Psalms, the book of Psalms, a book of the canon of the Old Testament.
scriptures: Jas 5:13
Is any among you afflicted? let him pray. Is any merry? let him sing psalms.
Psa 95:2
Let us come before his presence with thanksgiving, and make a joyful noise unto him with psalms.
Psa 47:7
For God is the King of all the earth: sing ye praises with understanding.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
corruption_summary: Marot put the Psalter into the people's voice, and the modern church's near abandonment of psalm-singing would have been unthinkable to the churches that sang his verses at the scaffold.
corruption_paragraphs: For the Reformed churches of the sixteenth century, the metrical psalm was the backbone of congregational praise: every member sang the whole Psalter through in the course of months, and children learned the psalms as they learned the catechism. Modern evangelical worship has replaced it almost entirely with contemporary songs, many of them shallow in content and individual in focus. The loss is not merely of a style but of a theology of praise shaped by God's own words.

The recovery need not take one side in the debate over exclusive psalmody. It is enough to restore the Psalms to the people's mouths again, sung with understanding, as Marot and Calvin did. A church that cannot sing Psalm 46 or Psalm 130 has lost something its fathers died singing.
roots_summary: Hebrew mizmor (H4210), psalm, melody; Greek psallo (G5567), to sing psalms; Hebrew sakal (H7919), to act with understanding.
roots_lines: Hebrew mizmor (H4210) — a psalm, song set to music; Psalm 95:2 (zemiroth).
Greek psallo (G5567) — to sing praise; James 5:13, Ephesians 5:19.
Hebrew maskil (H4905) — with understanding, a skilful song; Psalm 47:7.
usage: “Is any merry? let him sing psalms” (Jas 5:13) — the Genevan Psalter's warrant.
“make a joyful noise unto him with psalms” (Psa 95:2) — the congregation's song.
“sing ye praises with understanding” (Psa 47:7) — in French, not in Latin.

pos: n. (Jerome Bolsec, d. c. 1584, former Carmelite and physician who attacked Calvin's doctrine of predestination at Geneva in 1551, was banished, and later wrote a slanderous life of Calvin)
etymology: French Jérôme-Hermès Bolsec. His Life of Calvin (1577) was for centuries the source of Roman polemic against the Reformer.
biblical_def: Jerome Bolsec came to Geneva as a physician with Protestant sympathies. On 16 October 1551, at the weekly Bible study of the Genevan pastors called the Congregation, he rose and attacked the doctrine of predestination, saying it made God a tyrant and the author of sin. Calvin had come in unnoticed and answered him at length on the spot, citing Scripture and Augustine from memory. Bolsec was arrested; the council consulted the other Swiss churches, whose answers were less firm than Calvin wished, and in December banished him. The controversy led Calvin to write On the Eternal Predestination of God (1552) and the Genevan pastors to adopt a common statement. The doctrine Bolsec denied is Paul's: God “hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4); “as many as were ordained to eternal life believed” (Act 13:48). His objection was the one Paul answered: “Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God?” (Rom 9:20). Bolsec later returned to Rome and in 1577 published a Life of Calvin filled with invented vices, which Roman writers repeated for three centuries. The psalm is the answer to such books: “Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue” (Psa 120:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines slander as a false tale or report maliciously uttered, and tending to injure the reputation of another.
webster_full: SLANDER, n. A false tale or report maliciously uttered, and tending to injure the reputation of another by lessening him in the esteem of his fellow citizens.
2. Disgrace; reproach; disreputation.
scriptures: Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.
Rom 9:20
Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus?
Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue.
corruption_summary: Bolsec's slanders about Calvin's private life still circulate, and his objection to predestination — that it makes God a tyrant — is the standard objection in every evangelical church.
corruption_paragraphs: Bolsec's Life of Calvin accused him of gross immorality, greed and cruelty, without evidence; serious historians, Roman Catholic ones included, have long rejected it, yet its charges reappear in popular attacks on the Reformation and in anti-Calvinist polemic online. His theological objection has fared better: the claim that unconditional election makes God arbitrary and the author of sin is the first thing most Christians say when they meet the doctrine.

The recovery is Calvin's response in 1551 and the 1689 Confession's after him: God's decree is according to the most wise and holy counsel of His own will, freely and unchangeably, yet so that He is neither the author of sin nor is violence offered to the will of the creature. Paul's reply to the objector is still the first answer, and the honest reading of Calvin's life is the answer to the slander.
roots_summary: Greek eklegomai (G1586), to choose; tasso (G5021), to ordain, appoint; antapokrinomai (G470), to reply against.
roots_lines: Greek tasso (G5021) — to arrange, appoint, ordain; Acts 13:48.
Greek antapokrinomai (G470) — to answer back, contradict; Romans 9:20, Luke 14:6.
usage: “chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4) — the doctrine Bolsec attacked.
“who art thou that repliest against God?” (Rom 9:20) — Paul's answer to his objection.
“Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips” (Psa 120:2) — the answer to his Life of Calvin.

pos: n. (Sebastian Castellio, 1515–1563, humanist and former rector of the Geneva college, who after the execution of Servetus wrote Concerning Heretics against putting men to death for belief)
etymology: Latinised from French Châteillon or Castellion. Wrote under the pseudonym Martinus Bellius.
biblical_def: Sebastian Castellio was a gifted Latinist whom Calvin brought to Geneva as rector of its school in 1541. They fell out when Castellio denied that the Song of Solomon belonged in the canon, calling it a love poem, and questioned the article on Christ's descent into hell; refused ordination, he left for Basel in 1544, where he lived in poverty and later taught Greek. After Servetus was burned at Geneva in 1553, Castellio published Concerning Heretics (1554), a collection of testimonies against persecution, and later wrote that to kill a man is not to defend a doctrine but to kill a man. On that point he spoke Christ's mind: “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (Joh 18:36), and, to the disciples who would call down fire, “Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of” (Luk 9:55). Paul agrees: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4). But Castellio's remedy went further than Scripture. He made doctrinal uncertainty a virtue and regarded most disputed doctrines as too obscure to matter, and his treatment of the canon was the beginning of the same spirit. The canon is not his to judge: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines toleration as the act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved; and, specifically, the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to or different from those of the established church.
webster_full: TOLERATION, n. The act of tolerating; the allowance of that which is not wholly approved.
2. Specifically, the allowance of religious opinions and modes of worship in a state, when contrary to or different from those of the established church or belief.
scriptures: Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence.
Luk 9:55
But he turned, and rebuked them, and said, Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Castellio is now hailed as the prophet of modern tolerance against Calvin's intolerance; he was right that the sword cannot punish belief, and wrong that doctrine is too uncertain to be confessed.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern hero-narrative sets Castellio against Calvin as conscience against tyranny. On the execution of Servetus, the Reformed should be candid: the civil penalty for heresy, which Geneva shared with every state in Christendom, was wrong, and the 1689 Confession's teaching on liberty of conscience stands closer to Castellio's protest than to the magistrates of 1553. But modern tolerance is not Castellio's liberty of conscience; it is his scepticism, the belief that because Christians disagree, no doctrine can be certain enough to bind.

The recovery holds what he got right and refuses what he got wrong. No man is to be put to death for his belief; the church's weapons are the Word and the keys. And the Scriptures are clear enough to be confessed, the canon is God's and not the critic's, and certainty about the gospel is not cruelty but faith.
roots_summary: Greek basileia (G932), kingdom; sarkikos (G4559), carnal; theopneustos (G2315), given by inspiration of God.
roots_lines: Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed; 2 Timothy 3:16, the only use.
usage: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Joh 18:36) — what Castellio rightly urged after 1553.
“the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) — the church's only arms.
“All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16) — the canon he wrongly trimmed.

pos: n. (the Scottish National Covenant of 1638, signed at Greyfriars Kirk in Edinburgh, binding its subscribers to maintain the Reformed religion against Charles I's innovations in worship and government)
etymology: Latin convenire, to come together. Drafted by Alexander Henderson and Archibald Johnston of Wariston on the basis of the King's Confession of 1581.
biblical_def: The National Covenant was Scotland's answer to Charles I's attempt to impose a prayer book and canons modelled on the English church without the consent of the General Assembly. When the new liturgy was read in St Giles' in July 1637, the congregation rioted. In February 1638 nobles, ministers and people gathered at Greyfriars Kirk in Edinburgh to sign a covenant that renewed the King's Confession of 1581, listed the Acts of Parliament that established the Reformed church, and bound the subscribers before God to defend the true religion and forbear the novelties until they were tried in free assemblies. Copies went through the whole country, and hundreds of thousands signed, some, it is said, in their own blood. The pattern was Judah's under Asa: “they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul” (2Ch 15:12), and the returned exiles': “we make a sure covenant, and write it” (Neh 9:38). Its heart was the crown rights of Christ over His church, who is “the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18). The Glasgow Assembly that year abolished episcopacy, and the Solemn League and Covenant of 1643 carried the bond into England.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines covenant as a mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; and, in theology, the covenant of works and the covenant of grace.
webster_full: COVENANT, n. A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
2. A writing containing the terms of agreement or contract between parties.
3. In theology, the covenant of works and the covenant of grace.
scriptures: And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul;
Neh 9:38
And because of all this we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it.
Jer 50:5
They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten.
Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
corruption_summary: The National Covenant is remembered as a political revolt against a king; its signers understood it as a confession of Christ's sole headship over His church.
corruption_paragraphs: Secular history treats 1638 as an early constitutional rebellion, a stage in the wars of the three kingdoms, and modern evangelicals tend to regard national covenanting as a confusion of church and state. There is truth in the second point: a Baptist reading under the 1689 Confession does not hold that a nation can covenant itself into the church. But the core of the Covenant was not a political programme; it was the refusal to let a king order the worship of God by his own authority.

The recovery is that core: Christ alone is King and Head of His church, and neither monarch nor parliament may impose ceremonies on its worship or bishops on its government. The 1689 Confession confesses that the Lord Jesus is invested in a supreme and sovereign manner with all power for the calling, institution, order or government of the church. The Covenanters bled for that truth.
roots_summary: Hebrew berith (H1285), covenant; amanah (H548), a sure covenant, faithful agreement; Greek kephale (G2776), head.
roots_lines: Hebrew amanah (H548) — a firm agreement, sure covenant; Nehemiah 9:38.
usage: “they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers” (2Ch 15:12) — Greyfriars, 1638.
“we make a sure covenant, and write it” (Neh 9:38) — the signatures that went through Scotland.
“he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18) — the crown rights of Christ.

pos: n. (the conference at Poissy near Paris in September 1561, called by Catherine de' Medici, at which Theodore Beza presented the Reformed faith before the French court and bishops)
etymology: Latin colloquium, conversation, conference. Peter Martyr Vermigli also attended for the Reformed.
biblical_def: The Colloquy of Poissy was the regent Catherine de' Medici's attempt to reconcile the French church and the Huguenots by conference. Theodore Beza led the Reformed delegation, and on 9 September 1561 he addressed the young king, the queen mother, the princes and the assembled cardinals and bishops. He spoke with grace and learning, confessing the faith of the French churches, until he came to the Supper. There he said that Christ's body is as far removed from the bread and wine as the highest heaven is from the earth. The prelates rose in uproar, and the Cardinal of Tournon demanded that the king stop his ears. Beza's statement was the Reformed confession of Christ's ascension: “this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven” (Act 1:11), our High Priest “set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens” (Heb 8:1), “Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things” (Act 3:21). The conference failed; the Edict of January 1562 gave the Huguenots limited toleration, and within weeks the massacre of Vassy began the Wars of Religion. Beza had done what Peter commanded, given “a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines colloquy as conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; conference; dialogue.
webster_full: COLLOQUY, n. Conversation; mutual discourse of two or more; conference; dialogue.
scriptures: Act 1:11
Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.
Heb 8:1
Now of the things which we have spoken this is the sum: We have such an high priest, who is set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens;
Act 3:21
Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: Poissy is the model of every reconciliation conference that founders on the Supper, and Beza's sentence explains why: the ascension is not negotiable.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern ecumenical dialogues between Rome and Protestant bodies have produced agreed statements on justification and other topics, often by careful ambiguity. At Poissy the court wanted the same: a form of words both sides could sign. Beza refused to purchase peace with ambiguity. The question was where Christ's body is, and Scripture answers that it is in heaven, at the right hand of the Father, until He comes again.

The recovery is clarity spoken with courtesy. Beza did not insult his hearers; he told them plainly what the Reformed believe and why. The 1689 Confession confesses that the body and blood of Christ are not corporally or carnally present in the Supper but spiritually present to the faith of believers. A church that will not say so at a conference will soon not say so in its pulpit.
roots_summary: Greek analambano (G353), to take up; megalosune (G3172), majesty; apologia (G627), answer, defence.
roots_lines: Greek analambano (G353) — to take up, receive up; Acts 1:11, 1 Timothy 3:16.
usage: “taken up from you into heaven” (Act 1:11) — Beza's sentence at Poissy.
“set on the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in the heavens” (Heb 8:1) — where Christ's body is.
“a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15) — how Beza spoke.

pos: n. (the confession of faith of the Reformed churches of France, adopted at their first national synod in Paris in 1559 from a draft by Calvin, and confirmed at La Rochelle in 1571)
etymology: Latin Gallicanus, of Gaul, French. Also called the French Confession and, from 1571, the Confession of La Rochelle.
biblical_def: The Gallican Confession was adopted in secret by some twenty French Reformed churches gathered in Paris in May 1559, at the height of persecution under Henry II. Calvin had sent a draft of thirty-five articles; the synod enlarged it to forty. It opens with the one God revealed in His works and more clearly in His Word, lists the books of the canon by name, and confesses that they are known to be canonical not so much by the consent of the church as by the testimony and inward illumination of the Holy Spirit. That is the claim of Scripture itself: “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16), “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21), and believers receive it “not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God” (1Th 2:13); “My sheep hear my voice” (Joh 10:27). The confession goes on through the Trinity, creation, the fall, election, Christ's person and work, justification by faith, the church and the sacraments. At La Rochelle in 1571, with Beza presiding and Jeanne d'Albret, queen of Navarre, present, it was confirmed as the standard of the French churches.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confession as the act of acknowledging; and, in a religious sense, a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment; avowal of a fault, crime, debt or something that is against one's interest.
2. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed to be assented to or signed, as a preliminary to admission into a church.
scriptures: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.

For this cause also thank we God without ceasing, because, when ye received the word of God which ye heard of us, ye received it not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God, which effectually worketh also in you that believe.
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me:
corruption_summary: The Gallican Confession grounds the authority of Scripture in the Spirit's testimony, not the church's consent, and that article answers both Rome and the modern evangelical who rests the Bible on scholarship.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome holds that the church's authority establishes the canon and guarantees Scripture to the believer. Much modern evangelical apologetics rests the Bible's authority on manuscript evidence and historical argument, as though faith in God's Word must wait on scholars. The French confession, written by a persecuted church with no institutional power, put the ground where the Reformers found it: Scripture is self-authenticating, and the Spirit persuades God's people that it is His voice.

The 1689 Confession states the same truth: our full persuasion and assurance of the infallible truth and divine authority of Scripture is from the inward work of the Holy Spirit bearing witness by and with the Word in our hearts. Evidence has its place; it is not the foundation. Christ's sheep hear His voice.
roots_summary: Greek theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed; phero (G5342), to bear, move; akouo (G191), to hear.
roots_lines: Greek theopneustos (G2315) — given by inspiration of God; 2 Timothy 3:16.
Greek phero (G5342) — to bear along, move; 2 Peter 1:21.
usage: “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21) — the source of the canon.
“not as the word of men, but as it is in truth, the word of God” (1Th 2:13) — how the church receives it.
“My sheep hear my voice” (Joh 10:27) — the Spirit's testimony in the French confession.

pos: n. (John Cassian, c. 360–c. 435, monk who brought Egyptian monasticism to Gaul and taught that the first movement of the will toward God may come from man; the chief source of what was later called Semi-Pelagianism)
etymology: Latin Cassianus. Founder of monasteries at Marseilles; author of the Institutes and the Conferences.
biblical_def: John Cassian spent years among the desert monks of Egypt and afterward founded two monasteries at Marseilles, writing the Institutes on monastic life and the Conferences, dialogues with the desert fathers that shaped Western monasticism for a thousand years. In the thirteenth Conference he taught that although man cannot be saved without grace, the beginning of a good will is sometimes from man himself, and God then crowns it with help. Prosper of Aquitaine answered him in defence of Augustine. The Scriptures put the beginning with God: “without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5); “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God” (2Co 3:5); the good work is His from first to last, “he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it” (Php 1:6). Even the prayer for conversion is the cry of one God is already moving: “turn thou me, and I shall be turned” (Jer 31:18). The Second Council of Orange in 529 condemned the teaching that the beginning of faith is from ourselves, confessing that even the desire to be cleansed is wrought in us by the Spirit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines grace as the free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
webster_full: GRACE, n. Favour; good will; kindness.
2. Appropriately, the free unmerited love and favour of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
3. Favourable influence of God; divine influence or the influence of the Spirit, in renewing the heart and restraining from sin.
scriptures: Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;
Php 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:

I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself thus; Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the LORD my God.
corruption_summary: Cassian's middle way — grace needed, but man makes the first move — is the doctrine of most modern evangelism, which waits for the sinner to take the first step toward God.
corruption_paragraphs: Semi-Pelagianism is not a label for the far fringe. Cassian was a devout, orthodox-sounding monk who affirmed the necessity of grace and simply wanted room for human initiative. That is precisely the shape of popular evangelical theology: God has done His part, now you must do yours; He stands at the door and waits for you to open it. The Council of Orange condemned that shape of doctrine fourteen centuries ago, and the Reformation recovered Orange's verdict.

The recovery is the 1689 Confession on effectual calling: the call is of God's free and special grace alone, not from anything foreseen in man, who is altogether passive therein until he is quickened and renewed by the Holy Spirit. The sinner's first step toward God is God's step toward the sinner.
roots_summary: Greek hikanotes (G2426), sufficiency; enarchomai (G1728), to begin; Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn.
usage: “without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5) — against the beginning of good will from man.
“our sufficiency is of God” (2Co 3:5) — the verdict of Orange.
“turn thou me, and I shall be turned” (Jer 31:18) — conversion begun by God.
